chapter.title: Linux and Git
chapter.summary: The command line and version control: the two tools every engineer touches every day.

lessons.title: Linux and the shell: files, processes, permissions, pipes
lessons.summary: The filesystem layout, permissions, the process commands you use to debug production, pipes and text tools, shell scripting safely, and networking commands.

parts.label: Files and permissions
parts.body:
## Everything is a file

Linux presents devices, sockets, pipes and processes through the filesystem, so a small set of tools (`cat`, `grep`, `ls`) works on all of them. Absolute paths start at `/`.

| path | contents |
|---|---|
| `/etc` | system configuration |
| `/var/log` | logs (`journalctl` for systemd services) |
| `/home/<user>` | user files |
| `/tmp` | temporary files (may be cleared on reboot) |
| `/usr/bin`, `/bin` | commands |
| `/proc` | live kernel and process information (`/proc/<pid>/status`) |
| `/dev` | devices (`/dev/null` discards, `/dev/urandom` random bytes) |
| `/opt` | optional third-party software |

## Navigating and inspecting

```bash
pwd; ls -lah; cd /var/log             # where am I, list with sizes and hidden files
cat file; less file; head -n 20 f; tail -n 100 -f app.log   # follow a log live
find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime -1 -size +10M            # files by name, age, size
du -sh * | sort -h; df -h             # which directories are large; disk free per filesystem
stat file; file file; wc -l file      # metadata, type, line count
ln -s target link                     # symbolic link
```

## Permissions

Every file has an owner, a group and three permission triplets: user, group, other, each with **r**ead (4), **w**rite (2), e**x**ecute (1).

```
-rwxr-x---  1 alice devs 2048 Oct  5 10:00 deploy.sh
 │└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘
 │ │  │  └─ other: none
 │ │  └──── group (devs): read + execute (5)
 │ └─────── owner (alice): read + write + execute (7)
 └───────── file type: - file, d directory, l symlink
```

So that file is mode `750`. `chmod 750 f` or `chmod u+x,g-w f`; `chown alice:devs f`. For a directory, `r` lists names, `w` creates and deletes entries, `x` lets you enter/traverse it. Extras: **setuid** (run as the file's owner, e.g. `passwd`), **sticky bit** on `/tmp` (users can delete only their own files). `umask` sets default permissions for new files.

Principles: run services as dedicated non-root users, give files the least permissions that work, never `chmod 777`. `sudo` runs a command as root; keep it narrow.

## Users and SSH

`ssh user@host`, key-based authentication (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`, public key in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, private key `chmod 600`). Disable password login on servers. `scp`/`rsync -avz` copy files; `ssh -L 5432:db:5432 bastion` forwards a local port through a jump host.

parts.label: Processes, pipes and text
parts.body:
## Looking at what's running

```bash
ps aux | head; ps -ef --forest         # all processes (pid, user, cpu, mem, command)
top; htop                              # live view (sort by CPU/mem)
pgrep -af nginx; pkill -f myapp        # find / signal by name
kill -TERM 1234; kill -9 1234          # polite stop; force (can't be caught, no cleanup)
lsof -i :8080; ss -tulpn               # who is listening on which port
free -h; vmstat 1; iostat -x 1         # memory, system activity, disk I/O
uptime                                  # load average over 1, 5, 15 minutes
```

**Load average** is the average number of runnable (and uninterruptible) tasks. A load near the number of CPU cores is full; far above means queueing. Compare with CPU use: high load with low CPU usually means processes are waiting on I/O.

**Signals**: `SIGTERM` (15) asks a process to exit gracefully (apps should catch it and clean up), `SIGINT` (2, Ctrl-C), `SIGKILL` (9) cannot be caught, `SIGHUP` (often "reload config"), `SIGSTOP/SIGCONT` pause/resume. Prefer TERM, wait, then KILL.

**Background jobs**: `cmd &`, `jobs`, `fg`, `nohup cmd &` (survives logout), `tmux`/`screen` for persistent sessions. Real services belong under a supervisor: **systemd** (`systemctl status|start|restart|enable myapp`, unit files, `journalctl -u myapp -f`).

## Streams, redirection and pipes

Every process has stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2). 

```bash
cmd > out.txt          # stdout to file (overwrite);  >> append
cmd 2> err.txt         # stderr to file
cmd > all.txt 2>&1     # both to the same file (order matters)
cmd < input.txt        # file as stdin
cmd1 | cmd2            # stdout of cmd1 becomes stdin of cmd2
cmd > /dev/null 2>&1   # discard everything
```

## The text toolbox

```bash
grep -rn "ERROR" /var/log/app/            # search recursively with line numbers; -i ignore case; -v invert; -E regex
grep -c, -A3 -B3                          # count; context lines
awk '{print $1, $9}' access.log            # columns (default separator: whitespace)
awk '$9 >= 500 {n++} END {print n}' access.log   # conditional aggregation
sed 's/foo/bar/g' file; sed -i '' ...      # substitute (in place with -i)
cut -d, -f1,3 data.csv; sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head   # the frequency-count idiom
xargs -n1 -P4 cmd                          # run commands from a list, 4 in parallel
jq '.items[] | select(.status=="failed") | .id' resp.json   # JSON querying
tr, tee, column -t, paste, comm, diff
```

A classic one-liner, top 10 client IPs in an access log: `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10`.

## Debugging toolbox

`strace -p PID` (system calls), `ltrace`, `lsof -p PID` (open files), `tcpdump -i any port 443`, `curl -v`, `dig`, `traceroute`, `dmesg | tail` (kernel messages, OOM kills), `journalctl -xe`. When "the server is slow", check in order: load and CPU, memory and swap, disk space and I/O, network, then the application.

parts.label: Shell scripting safely
parts.body:
## Start every script defensively

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail          # exit on error, on unset variables, and fail a pipeline if any stage fails
IFS=$'\n\t'                # safer word splitting

trap 'echo "failed at line $LINENO" >&2' ERR
trap 'rm -rf "$tmpdir"' EXIT          # always clean up

tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
```

Key rules:

- **Quote variables**: `"$file"`, never `$file`, otherwise spaces and globs break things (and cause security bugs).
- Use `[[ ... ]]` for tests in bash; check arguments: `: "${1:?usage: $0 <env>}"`.
- Prefer `$(...)` over backticks. Use arrays for lists of arguments.
- Don't parse `ls`; use globs or `find -print0 | xargs -0`.
- Exit codes: `0` success, non-zero failure; `$?` holds the last. `cmd || exit 1`, `cmd && next`.
- Make scripts **idempotent** (safe to re-run): `mkdir -p`, `ln -sf`, check before creating.
- Use `shellcheck` in CI: it catches the majority of scripting bugs.
- When logic grows past ~50 lines or needs data structures, switch to Python or Node.

## cron and scheduling

`crontab -e`: `*/5 * * * * /opt/bin/job.sh >> /var/log/job.log 2>&1` (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week). Cron has a minimal environment (set PATH), no terminal, and overlapping runs unless you guard with `flock -n /tmp/job.lock`. systemd timers offer logging and dependencies. In the cloud prefer managed schedulers.

code.source:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Safe deploy helper: idempotent, quotes everything, cleans up, health-checks, rolls back
set -euo pipefail
: "${1:?usage: $0 <version>}"
version="$1"
app=/opt/myapp
releases="$app/releases"
tmp=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT

echo "Downloading $version..."
curl -fsSL "https://artifacts.example.com/myapp-$version.tar.gz" -o "$tmp/pkg.tgz"   # -f: fail on HTTP errors
mkdir -p "$releases/$version"
tar -xzf "$tmp/pkg.tgz" -C "$releases/$version"

prev=$(readlink -f "$app/current" || true)
ln -sfn "$releases/$version" "$app/current"        # atomic switch of the symlink
sudo systemctl restart myapp

for i in {1..20}; do                                # wait up to ~20 s for health
  if curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/healthz >/dev/null; then echo "healthy"; exit 0; fi
  sleep 1
done

echo "unhealthy, rolling back" >&2
[[ -n "$prev" ]] && ln -sfn "$prev" "$app/current" && sudo systemctl restart myapp
exit 1

# Everyday one-liners
du -ah /var | sort -rh | head -20                                  # biggest files/dirs
ss -tan state established | awk '{print $4}' | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
journalctl -u myapp --since "10 min ago" | grep -i error | tail    # recent errors from a service
find . -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -print0 | xargs -0 rm --            # delete old logs safely
watch -n2 'ss -s'                                                  # connection summary every 2 s
docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Status}}'                        # formatted output

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Linux fluency shows in **how you debug**: do you have a systematic way to find out why a server is slow, full, or unreachable?

## Questions with model answers

### 1. The server is slow. How do you investigate?

**Model answer.** Check the basics in order. `uptime` and `top` for load and CPU (high load with low CPU suggests I/O wait); `free -h` and `vmstat` for memory pressure and swapping; `df -h` and `iostat -x` for full or saturated disks; `ss -s` and `dmesg` for network and kernel issues (OOM kills); then application-level logs and metrics. I identify the saturated resource first (USE method), then which process uses it, then why.

### 2. Explain Linux file permissions: what does 755 mean?

**Model answer.** Three octal digits for owner, group and others, each the sum of read=4, write=2, execute=1. 755 is rwx for the owner and r-x for group and others: the owner can modify, everyone can read and execute. For directories, execute means permission to enter. I follow least privilege and avoid 777.

### 3. What's the difference between SIGTERM and SIGKILL?

**Model answer.** SIGTERM asks the process to terminate and can be caught so it can finish requests and clean up; SIGKILL is enforced by the kernel immediately, cannot be caught or ignored, and gives no chance to clean up. I send TERM first, wait a grace period, then KILL if necessary. Orchestrators like Kubernetes follow the same pattern.

### 4. What does `set -euo pipefail` do and why use it?

**Model answer.** `-e` exits on a failing command, `-u` treats unset variables as errors, and `pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails rather than only the last. Together they stop scripts from continuing after errors silently, such as `rm -rf "$DIR/"` with an empty `DIR`.

### 5. A disk is full. How do you find what's using space?

**Model answer.** `df -h` to find the full filesystem, `df -i` to rule out inode exhaustion, then `du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h` descending into the biggest directories. Common culprits: logs, Docker images/volumes, core dumps, deleted files still held open by a process (`lsof +L1`), which free space only after the process restarts. Then fix the cause: rotate logs, add retention, resize the disk.

### 6. How do you find which process is listening on port 8080?

**Model answer.** `ss -tulpn | grep 8080` or `lsof -i :8080`, which shows the PID and program (needs root for other users' processes). From the PID, inspect `ps -fp PID` and `/proc/PID`.

### 7. What does `2>&1` mean and why does order matter?

**Model answer.** It duplicates file descriptor 2 (stderr) onto wherever descriptor 1 (stdout) currently points. In `cmd > file 2>&1` stdout is redirected to the file first, then stderr follows it. In `cmd 2>&1 > file` stderr points to the terminal (the old stdout) and only stdout goes to the file.

## Rapid-fire

- **Show last 100 log lines and follow?** `tail -n 100 -f file`.
- **Count lines matching a pattern?** `grep -c pattern file`.
- **Replace text in a file in place (GNU)?** `sed -i 's/a/b/g' file`.
- **Run a command that survives logout?** `nohup`, tmux, or systemd.
- **What does load average 8 on a 4-core box mean?** About twice as many runnable tasks as cores: queueing.

keyPoints: Everything is a file; know /etc, /var/log, /proc and /dev, and use find, du and df to explore disk use.
Permissions are owner/group/other triplets of rwx (4-2-1); use least privilege, dedicated service users and never 777.
Debug slow servers with the USE method: load and CPU, memory, disk, network, then the application; ps, top, ss, lsof, journalctl and strace are the core tools.
Pipes and text tools (grep, awk, sed, sort, uniq, xargs, jq) turn logs into answers.
Write shell scripts with set -euo pipefail, quoted variables, traps for cleanup, idempotency and shellcheck.

options: Owner read/write, group read, others nothing
Owner read, group read/write, others execute
check.why: 6 = rw for the owner, 4 = r for the group, 0 = no access for others.

options: awk '{print $1}' file | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
check.q: Which command pipeline gives the most frequent values in column 1 of a file?
check.why: Extract the column, sort so duplicates are adjacent, count with uniq -c, then sort numerically descending.

options: Processes are blocked waiting on I/O
check.q: Load average is 12 on a 4-core server but CPU shows 90 percent idle. What is the likely cause?
check.why: Load counts tasks in uninterruptible I/O wait as well as runnable ones; high load with idle CPU points to a disk or network bottleneck.

lessons.title: Git in depth: the object model, branching, rebasing and recovery
lessons.summary: How Git stores history as a graph of commits, the staging area, merge versus rebase, collaboration workflows, and how to undo almost any mistake.

parts.label: The object model
parts.body:
## Git is a content-addressed graph

Git is not a list of file diffs. It stores **snapshots** in an object database, addressed by the SHA hash of their content. Four object types:

- **blob**: file contents.
- **tree**: a directory, listing names that point to blobs and other trees.
- **commit**: a snapshot (a pointer to a root tree) plus the author, message and **parent commit(s)**.
- **tag**: a named pointer (annotated tags add a message and signature).

A branch is just a **movable pointer to a commit** (a 41-byte file in `.git/refs/heads/`), and `HEAD` points to the current branch (or directly to a commit in "detached HEAD"). Making a commit creates a new commit object whose parent is the previous one, then moves the branch pointer forward. History is a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)**; branching is nearly free because it only creates a pointer.

Because hashes include the parent hashes, changing any old commit changes every descendant: that is why "rewriting history" produces new commits, and why shared history must not be rewritten casually.

## The three areas

```
working directory  --git add-->  staging area (index)  --git commit-->  repository (.git)
      (files)       <--git restore--                    <--git checkout/restore--
```

The **index** lets you assemble exactly what the next commit contains: `git add -p` stages individual hunks so each commit is one logical change. Check with `git status`, `git diff` (working vs index), `git diff --staged` (index vs HEAD).

## Daily commands

```bash
git status; git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git switch -c feature/x            # create and move to a branch (older: git checkout -b)
git add -p; git commit -m "Add rate limiter"
git fetch; git pull --rebase       # get remote changes, replay your commits on top
git push -u origin feature/x
git restore file                   # discard working changes;  git restore --staged file  unstage
git stash push -m "wip"; git stash pop
git blame file; git log -S"function name" --oneline    # who/when; find when a string was added
git bisect start; git bisect bad; git bisect good v1.2 # binary search for the commit that broke things
```

`git pull` = `fetch` + `merge` (or `rebase`). `fetch` only updates your remote-tracking branches (`origin/main`) and is always safe.

## Good commits

- One logical change per commit; the build and tests pass at each commit (so `bisect` works).
- Message: an imperative summary line of ~50 characters ("Add retry to payment client"), a blank line, then **why** the change was made (the diff already shows what).
- Don't commit secrets, build output or large binaries (`.gitignore`; use Git LFS for big files). If a secret is committed, rotate it: deleting the commit is not enough.
- Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`) help automate changelogs and releases.

parts.label: Merge, rebase and workflows
parts.body:
## Merge

`git merge feature` joins two lines of history. If the target hasn't diverged it **fast-forwards** (just moves the pointer). Otherwise Git creates a **merge commit** with two parents, preserving the true shape of history.

When both sides changed the same lines you get a **conflict**: Git marks the file with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`; you edit the result, `git add`, and continue. A 3-way merge uses the **merge base** (common ancestor) to decide: if only one side changed a region, take that change.

## Rebase

`git rebase main` (on a feature branch) takes your commits, and **replays them one by one on top of main**, creating *new* commits with new hashes. The result is a linear history as if you started from the latest main.

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| history | preserves branches and merge commits (accurate) | linear (clean) |
| rewrites commits | no | yes (new hashes) |
| conflicts | resolved once | may need resolving per replayed commit |
| safe on shared branches | yes | **no** |

**The golden rule: never rebase commits that others have based work on** (anything already pushed to a shared branch). Rebase your own private feature branch freely; then force-push with `git push --force-with-lease` (refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime), never plain `--force`.

**Interactive rebase** `git rebase -i HEAD~5` lets you reorder, **squash**, reword or drop commits to clean up before review. `git commit --fixup` + `git rebase -i --autosquash` makes it easy.

**Squash merge** (GitHub option) collapses a PR into one commit on main: tidy history, lost granularity. **Cherry-pick** (`git cherry-pick <sha>`) copies a single commit to the current branch (hotfix backports).

## Branching strategies

| strategy | idea | fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Trunk-based development** | everyone integrates into `main` at least daily, short-lived branches, feature flags hide unfinished work, strong CI | teams that deploy continuously (best correlated with high delivery performance) |
| **GitHub Flow** | feature branch → pull request → review → merge to main → deploy | web apps and SaaS |
| **Gitflow** | long-lived `develop`, release and hotfix branches | scheduled releases, multiple supported versions (heavier) |

Long-lived branches cause painful merges. Prefer small PRs (under ~400 lines), frequent integration, protected `main` (required reviews and passing checks), and CODEOWNERS.

## Pull request practice

Describe what and why, link the issue, keep it focused, self-review the diff first, respond to comments with commits (or fixups), and don't merge red CI. Reviewers should look for correctness, tests, naming, security and operability, and be kind and specific.

parts.label: Undoing mistakes
parts.body:
Git rarely loses committed work. Know which tool fits:

| situation | command |
|---|---|
| discard uncommitted changes to a file | `git restore file` |
| unstage | `git restore --staged file` |
| fix the last commit message or add forgotten files | `git commit --amend` (only if unpushed) |
| undo a commit **on a shared branch** by adding an inverse commit | `git revert <sha>` |
| move the branch back (local history) | `git reset --soft HEAD~1` keep changes staged; `--mixed` (default) keep as working changes; `--hard` throw changes away |
| committed to the wrong branch | `git switch right-branch; git cherry-pick <sha>`, then `git reset --hard HEAD~1` on the wrong one |
| "I lost a commit after a hard reset or bad rebase" | `git reflog` shows where HEAD has been; `git switch -c rescue <sha>` |
| remove a file from history (secret leaked) | rotate the secret first; then `git filter-repo`; force-push; tell collaborators |
| a merge went wrong | `git merge --abort` / `git rebase --abort`, or `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` |

The **reflog** records every position of HEAD for ~90 days, which is why almost nothing is truly lost. `reset --hard` and `git clean -fd` do destroy **uncommitted** work, so look before you run them.

## Handy extras

- **Worktrees**: `git worktree add ../hotfix main` checks out another branch in a second folder without stashing.
- **Hooks** (`pre-commit`, `commit-msg`): run linters/tests before committing (manage with husky or pre-commit).
- **Submodules** and **subtrees** for embedding repos (use sparingly; monorepo tooling is often better).
- **Signed commits** (`-S`) prove authorship; **tags** mark releases (`git tag -a v1.4.0 -m ...`, semver).
- **Shallow and partial clones** (`--depth 1`, `--filter=blob:none`) speed up CI on large repos.

code.source:
# A realistic feature flow
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git switch -c feature/rate-limit

# ...work, commit in logical steps...
git add -p && git commit -m "Add token bucket limiter"
git add -p && git commit -m "Wire limiter into API middleware"

# Before opening the PR: sync with main and tidy history
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main                 # replay my commits on the latest main
git rebase -i origin/main              # squash fixups, reword messages
git push --force-with-lease -u origin feature/rate-limit

# Recover from a bad reset
git reflog                             # find the lost commit, e.g. 3f2a9c1
git switch -c rescue 3f2a9c1

# Find the commit that introduced a bug
git bisect start HEAD v1.4.0
git bisect run npm test                # automates good/bad; ends at the first bad commit
git bisect reset

parts.label: Interview
parts.body:
## What interviewers are testing

Fluency shows in explaining **what Git does underneath** and in recovering from mistakes without panic.

## Questions with model answers

### 1. Merge vs rebase: when do you use each?

**Model answer.** Merge preserves the true history with a merge commit and never rewrites commits, so it is safe on shared branches. Rebase replays my commits on top of the latest base to get a linear history and clean PRs, but creates new commits, so I only use it on my own unpublished (or private feature) branches and push with `--force-with-lease`. I rebase to update a feature branch and merge or squash-merge the PR into main per team policy.

### 2. What is the difference between `git reset` and `git revert`?

**Model answer.** `reset` moves the branch pointer (and optionally the index and working tree) to an earlier commit, rewriting local history; it is for unpublished work. `revert` creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an earlier one, leaving history intact, which is what you want on shared branches such as main.

### 3. What is a detached HEAD?

**Model answer.** HEAD pointing directly at a commit instead of a branch name, as when checking out a tag or an old commit. New commits are not on any branch, so they can be lost when you switch away; create a branch (`git switch -c name`) to keep them.

### 4. You accidentally ran `git reset --hard` and lost commits. What now?

**Model answer.** Run `git reflog` to list where HEAD has been, find the commit hash from before the reset, and create a branch or reset to it. Committed work is recoverable through the reflog for a long time; only uncommitted changes destroyed by `--hard` are gone.

### 5. How does Git store data? Is it diffs?

**Model answer.** It stores snapshots as content-addressed objects: blobs for file contents, trees for directories, commits pointing to a tree and to parent commits. Identical content is stored once, and packfiles compress objects using deltas for storage efficiency, but conceptually each commit is a full snapshot. Branches and tags are lightweight pointers to commits.

### 6. Fast-forward merge versus merge commit?

**Model answer.** If the target branch hasn't moved since the feature branched, Git can simply advance its pointer (fast-forward), keeping history linear without a merge commit. If both have diverged a three-way merge creates a merge commit with two parents. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit to record that a feature branch existed.

### 7. How do you resolve a merge conflict well?

**Model answer.** Understand both sides' intent (use `git log`, the PR descriptions or ask the author), edit the file to a correct combination, run tests, stage and continue. Prefer smaller, more frequent merges to avoid big conflicts, and use `rerere` or a merge tool for repeated conflicts. After resolving, verify the build because a textually clean merge can still be semantically broken.

## Rapid-fire

- **Safe force push?** `--force-with-lease`.
- **Show history graph?** `git log --oneline --graph --all`.
- **Combine last 3 commits?** `git rebase -i HEAD~3` and squash.
- **Find who changed a line?** `git blame`.
- **Find the bad commit automatically?** `git bisect run`.

keyPoints: Git stores content-addressed snapshots (blobs, trees, commits); branches are movable pointers and history is a DAG, so branching is cheap.
The index lets you build commits deliberately; make small logical commits that each build.
Merge preserves history; rebase rewrites it into new commits, so never rebase shared commits and use --force-with-lease.
Trunk-based development with short-lived branches and strong CI beats long-lived branches.
The reflog and revert/reset make mistakes recoverable; rotate any leaked secret rather than only deleting it.

options: git reset --hard HEAD~1 and force push

check.why: revert adds a new inverse commit without rewriting shared history, so collaborators are not disrupted.
